In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the pro-inflammatory gene expression in GBM and with the demonstration that GBM-SC, under hypoxic conditions, acquire an invasive and migrative behavior.
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the acquisition of the pro-inflammatory phenotype in human solid gliobastoma and in GBM- SCs.
the role of hypoxic and inflammatory conditions in glioma progression and the potential use of this knowledge for the identification of new therapeutic approaches.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the pro-inflammatory gene signature in GBM is a consequence of hypoxia and that this signature is a marker of the invasive/migratory phenotype of hypoxic glioblastoma stem cells, which is lost after their differentiation.

the inflammatory response in glioblastoma is not simply a bystander effect but a key component in glioma progression and that this response is mediated by the tumor microenvironment and the tumor stem cells.
the hypoxic and the inflammatory microenvironment in solid gliobastomas is a relevant factor in the progression toward a malignant phenotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hypoxia is able to promote the inflammatory phenotype in GBM stem/progenitor cells, thus favoring tumor growth and invasion.
the inflammatory phenotype of GBM-SC is acquired under hypoxic conditions, and that the inflammatory phenotype is lost when these cells differentiate.
in hypoxic GBM-SC a coordinated pro-inflammatory gene expression is induced, which may contribute to malignant progression of the tumor, through a gain of invasive/migratory function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proinflammatory response is not a mere bystander in glioblastomas; instead, it may be a critical factor in the development of the malignant phenotype of glioblastomas.
the hypoxic microenvironment in solid tumors may be a key element for tumor progression.
hypoxia may be a relevant stimulus for the acquisition of an aggressive phenotype in glioblastoma stem cells.
